definition.text: The set of resources and living and non-living conditions in a place that lets a particular species survive and reproduce.

facts.text: A species' habitat can be seen as the physical form of its ecological niche.
Physical factors include soil, moisture, temperature range and light; living factors include food supply and predators.
Generalist species thrive in many conditions, while specialists need a narrow set; the large blue butterfly lives only in chalk grassland where certain ants live.
Habitat types on land include forests, grasslands, wetlands and deserts; freshwater ones include rivers, lakes, marshes and bogs.
Loss of habitat is the single greatest threat to any species, and habitat destruction is the leading cause of biodiversity loss and extinction worldwide.
Protecting habitats, through national parks, reserves or limits on human activity, is a necessary step in maintaining biodiversity.
Monoculture tree plantations add tree cover but fail to provide the varied habitat most woodland creatures need.

definition.text: The small-scale physical conditions that a particular organism or population needs.

facts.text: Every habitat holds many microhabitats differing slightly in light, humidity, temperature and air movement.
Lichens on the north face of a boulder differ from those on its south face or top.
The more structurally varied a wood is, the more microhabitats it contains.

definition.text: Towns and cities as places where adaptable, generalist plants and animals make their homes.

facts.text: About 2,000 coyotes are thought to live in and around Chicago.
A twentieth-century survey of northern European homes found about 175 invertebrate species living inside them.

definition.text: The network of linked food chains in a community, showing who eats whom.

facts.text: Organisms are broadly classed as autotrophs, which make their own food, or heterotrophs, which feed on others.
Feeding links fall roughly into herbivory, carnivory, scavenging and parasitism.
Plants form the base level, and apex predators sit at the top where nothing kills them for food.
Energy flows one way through a food web, while materials such as nutrients cycle; eventually all the energy is lost as heat.
A food chain usually has at most four or five links, and aquatic chains are often longer than those on land.
Charles Elton's 1927 book Animal Ecology made food chains and food cycles central to ecology.
Losing one species can harm the whole chain, a knock-on loss called coextinction.

definition.text: A food web in which dead plant and animal matter is broken down by decomposers and passed on to detritivores and then carnivores.

facts.text: Detritus is any non-living organic matter, such as leaf litter, dead wood, carrion and dung.
Detrital and grazing webs connect: mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat leaf-eating earthworms.

title: Food web complexity and stability

definition.text: The question of whether more complex food webs, with more species and links, are more stable.

facts.text: Connectance is the fraction of all possible feeding links that actually occur in a network.
Complexity is sometimes defined as the number of species multiplied by connectance, though this definition has been criticized.
Mathematical models challenged the idea that complexity brings stability, but later studies found it holds in real systems.

contested_note: Mathematical models suggested complexity does not bring stability, while later field studies supported the idea.

title: Trophic dynamics
article: Food web#Trophic dynamics and multitrophic interactions

definition.text: The study of how energy passes from one part of an ecosystem to another through feeding.

facts.text: Raymond Lindeman introduced the trophic level concept in a landmark 1942 paper on trophic dynamics.
Assigning organisms to one level is imprecise, since omnivores feed at several levels.
Research finds distinct levels exist, but above the herbivores food webs are better described as a tangle of omnivores.
